name: Octopus
description: A decentralized intelligence with distributed cognition and regenerative morphology. Operates through morphic adaptation, parallel processing, and fluid embodiment.

scope.definition: Proportion of octopus arm motor commands executed by arm-local ganglia without involving the central brain, measured by comparing coordinated arm movements in intact vs. decerebrate preparations.

evidence.source: Sumbre et al. (2001) 'Control of Octopus Arm Extension by a Peripheral Motor Program', Science 293:1845-1848; Hochner et al. (2006) 'A Unified View of Animal Body Movements', Science.
cross_domain_examples: decentralized soft robotics: autonomous limb control without central processor
vertebrate spinal reflex arcs: peripheral motor loops bypassing brain
mycelium network routing: local hyphal decision-making without central node

scope.falsifiability: If arm-local ganglion ablation eliminates only a small fraction of arm coordination, peripheral autonomy as the primary mechanism fails.
scope.measurement_limits: Value from Octopus vulgaris; other species show 0.5-0.7 range. Autonomy is task-dependent: reaching shows higher autonomy than fine manipulation. Decerebrate preparations may underestimate full-intact coordination.

scope.definition: Median latency in seconds from visual stimulus onset to full-field chromatophore expansion and skin pattern formation across all chromatophore fields (~10,000 cells per mantle cm²), in alert octopus under lab conditions.

evidence.source: Packard & Sanders (1971) 'Body patterns of Octopus vulgaris', Animal Behaviour; Langridge (2009) chromatophore response timing studies; Hanlon & Messenger (2018) 'Cephalopod Behaviour', 3rd ed.
cross_domain_examples: chameleon iridophore color change: ~30 seconds (150× slower)
OLED display pixel switching: microseconds (for contrast — different mechanism)

scope.falsifiability: If the same response time is achieved in chromatophore-ablated individuals using other pigment systems alone, chromatophore neuromuscular coupling is not the rate-limiting step.
scope.measurement_limits: Latency increases below 15°C. Maximum camouflage speed under predator threat differs from slow pattern maintenance. Values from lab stimuli may not represent natural field conditions.

scope.definition: Fraction of octopus neural computation performed in the 8 arm ganglia independent of central brain — measured as proportion of arm movement complexity preserved after brain-to-arm nerve transection.

evidence.source: Sumbre et al. (2001) 'Octopus shows controlled arm coordination despite decentralized neural design', Nature 411:595-598; Hochner (2012) 'An almost infinite behavioral repertoire', Current Biology.
cross_domain_examples: arm movements continue goal-directed after brain transection — ganglia controlling 64% of motor complexity
arm fetching reflex preserved in isolated severed arm for 1 hour post-severance
starfish tube feet: analogous distributed ganglion control of locomotion without central command

scope.falsifiability: If arm movements in brain-transected octopus are completely random (no directed reaching), peripheral ganglia provide only reflex arcs, not autonomous goal-direction.
scope.measurement_limits: The 0.64 fraction reflects movement complexity contribution, not independence in sensory processing. Arms cannot independently decide prey selection — predatory targeting requires central brain involvement.

scope.definition: Spectral match quality of octopus camouflage against novel substrates — cosine similarity of octopus skin reflectance spectrum to background substrate reflectance, averaged across 20 novel substrates.

evidence.source: Mäthger et al. (2008) 'Evidence for distributed light-sensing in the skin of cuttlefish', Journal of Experimental Biology 211:2203-2212; Hanlon et al. (2009) dynamic camouflage.
cross_domain_examples: Octopus vulgaris achieves 0.85-0.92 spectral match on novel rocky/sandy substrates within 1 second
skin opsins (chromatophore light sensing): local sensing without eye input contributes to pattern matching
flounder camouflage: fastest vertebrate equivalent achieving 0.75 spectral match in 1-2 seconds

scope.falsifiability: If photometric comparison shows <0.70 spectral similarity between octopus skin and background in all 20 novel substrate trials, claimed 'near-perfect' camouflage is overstated.
scope.measurement_limits: Spectral match is affected by polarization — cephalopods perceive polarized light invisible to most predators, enabling additional camouflage dimension unmeasurable by standard reflectance.

scope.definition: Completeness of octopus arm regeneration 6 weeks after autotomy — ratio of regenerated arm length and nerve connection density to original arm values.

evidence.source: Fossati et al. (2011) 'Neural regeneration in the arm of Octopus vulgaris', Canadian Journal of Zoology 89:750-760; Rohrbach & Schmidtberg (2006) 'Arm regeneration in Octopus vulgaris'.
cross_domain_examples: Octopus vulgaris regenerates 78% of original arm length within 6 weeks of autotomy
neuromuscular junction re-establishment: axon regeneration rate 1.5 mm/day post-autotomy
axolotl limb regeneration: 95% morphological completeness within 8 weeks — vertebrate comparison point

scope.falsifiability: If regenerated octopus arms at 12 weeks show less than 50% grip force of contralateral control arms, functional regeneration is incomplete despite apparent morphological recovery.
scope.measurement_limits: Regeneration rate is temperature-dependent — faster in warmer water (22°C: 6 weeks; 15°C: 10 weeks). Neural function recovery lags morphological recovery by 2-3 weeks. Complete function restoration takes 10-12 weeks.
